method: Trained at hospital A, frozen, then tested once at hospital B.
headline: The official score fell from 0.368 at home to 0.238 at the second hospital.
finding: At hospital B, 109 of 1,142 sepsis patients (9.5%) got their first alert in the 12 hours before onset. Another 377 were alerted earlier than that, and 656 were missed. It raised a false alarm on 1,358 of 18,858 patients who never developed sepsis (7.2%, against the 15% budget set at hospital A). The official utility score fell from 0.368 at hospital A dev (the calibration set) to 0.238 at hospital B. A model that sees only hours in the unit scored 0.242 there.

limits:
Hospital B, 20,000 patients. These are retrospective results on recorded data, not performance in clinical use.

- **Timely catches are rare.** Of 1,142 sepsis patients, 109 (9.5%) got their first alert in the 12 hours before onset. 377 (33.0%) were alerted earlier than that. 656 (57.4%) were missed.
- **False alarms.** 1,358 of 18,858 patients who never developed sepsis were alerted at least once (7.2%). That is 12.5 false alarms per timely catch. This counts patients, not alerts.
- **Workload.** 115 alerts per 1,000 patient-days, and 0.9 repeat alerts per alerted patient.
- **It did not beat the clock.** A model that sees only hours in the unit scored utility 0.242. The full model scored 0.238.
- **First-day sepsis.** When the sepsis label starts before hour 24, 57 of 514 patients were alerted by onset (11.1%), against 429 of 628 (68.3%) when it starts later.
- **Late-entry cases** (label already on in the first recorded hour): the model caught 14 of 223. The modified SIRS rule caught 150 of 223.
- **Hospital A dev numbers are calibration numbers.** The alert line was set on those 4,068 patients, so their 15.0% false alarm share is true by construction, not a measured result.
- **The score is not a probability.** It is the model's output divided by the frozen alert cutoff. Calibration was not checked.

The group with the lowest share alerted by onset is **80 and over**. This is a first check, not a fairness audit. The data has no race, ethnicity, language or insurance fields, so those groups cannot be checked at all.

local_curve.caption: After-the-fact: this was run after the hospital B result, so it is not part of the frozen test. Hospital B was cut once into 10,000 local patients to learn from and 10,000 test patients (571 with sepsis) that no model trained on. Each point is a model trained on 16,268 hospital A training patients plus that many local ones. Each alert cutoff was set on the scored test patients themselves, at a 25% false alarm cap, the same way for every point. So this shows the shape of the curve. It is not a score to quote. The first 1,000 local patients close 52% of the gap between none (0.262) and 10,000 (0.385). A model trained on the 10,000 local patients alone, with no hospital A data, scored 0.399. One split, so small gaps are not settled.
